analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling in parts of the Gulf of Mexico near Florida.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have permanently banned oil and gas leasing off Florida's Gulf coast, never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee at the end of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal law to permanently extend the existing ban on offshore oil and gas leasing, preleasing, and related activities in certain areas of the Gulf of Mexico, closing those waters to energy companies for good. Under current law, that protection is temporary and could be changed by a future Congress. The bill never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, residents and visitors of Florida's Gulf coast would gain permanent protection against offshore drilling near their shores, including the tourism and fishing economies that depend on clean water and beaches. The public broadly would keep those waters off-limits to energy development indefinitely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal residents and tourism economies

how_it_helps.text: It amends the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act of 2006 to permanently extend the existing moratorium on oil and gas leasing, preleasing, and related activities in certain areas of the Gulf of Mexico, rather than letting it lapse on its current expiration schedule.

By making the ban permanent, it prevents future administrations from opening those waters to drilling leases, protecting Florida's Gulf beaches, fishing grounds, and tourism economy from the risk of spills.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would bear the cost, losing permanent access to those Gulf areas for exploration and drilling. Any cost to consumers would come through marginally reduced future domestic energy supply.

drawbacks.text: Permanently barring drilling in those Gulf waters removes a potential future source of domestic oil and gas production, which the energy industry argues could mean somewhat higher reliance on drilling elsewhere or on imports.
The moratorium applies only to certain areas of the Gulf, so it protects Florida's coastline but leaves other Gulf waters — and the communities near them — open to leasing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a permanent legal shield for Florida's Gulf coastline against offshore drilling spills — is broad and durable, and the cost to consumers is negligible since the protected waters were never a major part of U.S. production. The bill was simple, one sentence long, and hard to argue was badly designed. The drawback is purely distributional: it forecloses future domestic energy development in those waters and would have been contested by oil and gas producers. On balance, the protections it promised outweighed the costs, which makes its quiet death more consequential.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee it was sent to never acted on it, so it died quietly when the congressional session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 11, 2018 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
Six days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests are better off, because the waters the bill would have permanently closed to drilling remain available for future leasing decisions. Florida's coastal communities gain nothing, since the underlying moratorium can still lapse under existing law.

for.name: Rep. Francis Rooney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought to permanently extend the Gulf drilling moratorium.

for.name: 13 House Republicans and 1 House Democrat (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, signaling support for a permanent drilling ban.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Offshore drilling companies and industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed permanent expansions of drilling bans in the Gulf of Mexico during this period.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's cosponsorship was heavily Republican — 13 Republicans and 1 Democrat — reflecting its Florida-focused, anti-drilling appeal across party lines in that state.

industries.note: The bill would permanently close off certain Gulf of Mexico waters to oil and gas leasing and exploration, removing future drilling opportunities. Those areas stay protected instead, and coastal residents avoid spill risk.
A permanent drilling ban protects beaches, fisheries, and tourism revenue from the risk of oil spills like the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster. The bill would have locked in that protection.
